idiom_name: try? expression (converting errors to optional values)
implementation_notes: Swift absorbs the mute into the language: `try?` evaluates a throwing expression and converts any thrown error into nil - the book's own section title is 'Converting Errors to Optional Values' - so the classic do/catch structure collapses into one keyword and nothing propagates. When the ignored type must be pinned down or the failure should leave a trace, use the classic form `do { try call() } catch let error as SpecificError { /* documented */ } catch { throw error }`, which rethrows everything that was not analysed. Discarding the value of a non-Void `try?` mutes the result as well as the failure, so make that explicit with `_ = try? ...`.
pitfalls: `try?` collapses every failure of the expression to nil: cancellation, permission and disk errors become indistinguishable, so when the caller could act on any of them the do/catch form with a typed catch is required.

Discarding a non-Void `try?` result mutes the value too (`try? buffer.write(to:)` drops the byte count); use `_ = try?` deliberately and keep `try!`/force-unwrap out of the same expression so tolerated and fatal failures do not blur.
In property initializers, deinit paths or lazy defaults the `try?` may run at an unpredictable time (during teardown), where the context that justified the mute no longer exists.
